activities.anchor: the whole discipline of development geography lives in
activities.caption: drag the divider — the money and the life
activities.name: devLivingCompare

config.prompt: The two ideas that usually travel together — drag the divider:

before.label: standard of living
before.text: What money buys: income, goods, housing. Easy to measure, easy to average — and easy to fake with a single large number.

after.label: quality of life
after.text: How good living actually is: health, education, security, a clean environment. Harder to count — and the 'not always' between this and income is where the whole discipline lives.

config.why: The gaps run between countries and inside them — and the inside-country gaps are often the larger political fact.

activities.caption: file each indicator: money, or life
activities.name: devIndicatorBuckets

config.prompt: Economic or social? File each development indicator:

items.label: GNI per capita (with remittances earned abroad)

config.why: The Human Development Index blends one from each family into a geometric mean — and the money-only LIC/MIC/HIC sorting is what the social indicators constantly correct.

activities.anchor: Costa Rica outlives several countries twice as rich
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the scatter's secret
activities.name: devScatterPredict

config.q: The USA earns far more per person than Japan, yet lives about four years shorter. What does that scatter around the Preston curve tell you?
choices: The Preston curve is unreliable — the points should line up
Income is a means; converting it into health and schooling is the development story
Japan's numbers must be a statistical error
config.why: The curve flattens — the first few thousand dollars buy enormous gains (clean water, vaccines, clinics), the next fifty thousand buy very few — and how a country converts income is the real story.

activities.name: devHdiOrder

config.prompt: Rank these by HDI score, lowest first:
config.why: Computed by hand from Niger's figures (life expectancy about 62, roughly 2 years of schooling, $1,700 GNI) you get ≈ 0.40 against the published 0.394 — the formula is short enough to run on paper.

activities.caption: pin the Gini — the world's most uneven spread
activities.name: devGiniPlace

config.prompt: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person owning everything). South Africa — the world's highest — sits where?
config.why: About 0.63, the world's highest — one of the alternatives to averages, alongside the MPI, which found about 1.1 billion people poor across health, schooling and living standards at once.

activities.anchor: come in three flavours, and strong answers use them together
activities.caption: pair each cause with its flavour
activities.name: devUnevenMatch

config.prompt: Why development is uneven — pair each piece of evidence with its family of reasons:

pairs.left: ports for exports and railways from mine to coast
pairs.right: historical-economic — colonial economies built to extract

pairs.left: a dozen African countries landlocked, much of the Sahel
pairs.right: physical — every export crosses a neighbour's politics

pairs.left: South Sudan fell from the mid-0.5s HDI to 0.381 after 2011
pairs.right: social-political — conflict destroys in a year what decades built

pairs.left: the schooling of girls, throttling everything downstream
pairs.right: social-political — the single most-supported intervention in development economics

config.why: Geography is not destiny — Japan proved that on resource-poor islands — but it sets the bill; strong answers use the three flavours together.

activities.anchor: The pattern (8.2.2) is no longer the neat
activities.caption: call the magnitude — history's largest lift
activities.name: devChinaEstimate

config.prompt: China's growth since 1978 lifted roughly how many people out of extreme poverty?
config.why: About 800 million — the largest poverty reduction in history, and proof that the old map's weakness was implying the poor stay poor: South Korea was poorer than Ghana in 1960 and is now high-income.
config.context: The sharpest gaps are now internal: Kerala achieves 75+ life expectancy on modest income, while China's coastal provinces would rank HIC and its western provinces MIC.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the Vietnam case note
activities.name: devVietnamSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Vietnam case note is wrong — click it:
lines: Vietnam was desperately poor in 1986 when the Doi Moi reforms began.
It opened to markets, stabilised inflation, and invested ferociously in schooling and ports.
Poverty fell from nearly 60 per cent in the early 1990s to under 5 per cent today.
The convergence was driven mainly by aid transfers from donor countries.
Its HDI has climbed to 0.726, with growth of roughly 6–7 per cent a year.
config.correction: The recipe was trade plus education plus stable government — not aid; dependency on transferred money can hollow out local accountability.
config.why: Vietnam is the counterexample to every 'poor countries stay poor' reflex: the gap closed by policy, consistently applied — with trade-offs (environmental pressure, one-party politics) a full answer should name.
